enrichment.short_title: Entertainu v Secretary of State: hostess bar planning and enforcement appeals

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Control of Advertisements) Regulations 1992

key_facts: Entertainu operated a hostess bar in the basement of 26 Wardour Street, Soho; Westminster refused planning permission and issued an enforcement notice.
A replacement inspector dismissed appeals under policy TACE 13, finding the use harmed the character of the Soho Conservation Area through outdoor advertising and a distinctive entrance.
The claimant argued signage was excluded from the inquiry, natural justice was breached, and parallel advertisement consent regime should have been addressed.
Richards J refused late amendments on parallel-regime and conditions points and dismissed both the section 288 challenge and section 289 appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court challenge under section 288 and appeal under section 289 against a planning inspector's decision refusing planning permission and upholding an enforcement notice.
enrichment.outcome: Challenge and appeal dismissed; Secretary of State awarded summary assessed costs of £5,340; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Signage and external appearance were relevant planning considerations despite a separate advertisement consent regime; an inspector's professional judgment on character and a distinctive entrance will not be quashed unless irrational; late new grounds raising parallel-regime arguments may properly be refused where they would require adjournment and lack prior notice.
legal_issues: Whether signage was excluded from the inspector's inquiry by agreement
Whether reliance on signage breached natural justice
Whether the inspector had to address the parallel advertisements regime explicitly
Whether the inspector's finding of a distinctive obtrusive entrance was irrational
linked_authorities: Gateshead Metropolitan Borough Council v Secretary of State for the Environment [1994] 1 PLR 85
Fairmount Investments Ltd v Secretary of State for the Environment [1976] 1 WLR 1255

enrichment.short_title: Erdogan v SSHD: asylum credibility after partial adjudicator error
key_facts: Kurdish Alevi appellant left Turkey in January 2002 claiming asylum after alleged arrest over a Kurdish-language petition.
Adjudicator Bryan disbelieved the January 2002 account partly because petition activity seemed implausible while Kurdish language use was restricted.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal accepted that reasoning could not stand but upheld disbelief on other credibility findings including lack of dedicated HADEP support and delayed departure.
The Court of Appeal held the tribunal's overall decision remained within reasonable bounds despite the adjudicator's admitted error.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision dismissing an asylum appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; publicly funded costs subject to detailed assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Where part of an adjudicator's credibility reasoning is shown wrong, the tribunal may still uphold refusal if remaining findings provide a reasonable basis; asylum credibility is a composite question and findings must be read as a whole rather than compartmentalised hermetically.
legal_issues: Effect of an admitted error in part of the adjudicator's credibility findings
Whether remaining findings supported refusal of asylum
Risk on return to Turkey for a non-dedicated political supporter

enrichment.short_title: Sahardid v Camden: homelessness review date and allocation policy
key_facts: Homeless Somali mother with priority need sought two-bedroom accommodation from Camden on medical grounds; Camden offered a one-bedroom flat at 10 Webheath.
Camden's allocations scheme entitled families with a child over five to two-bedroom properties; the appellant's son turned five three days before the November 2003 review letter.
The reviewing officer did not address the child's age or the published five-year policy in the review decision.
The County Court upheld Camden but the Court of Appeal held failure to apply the allocation scheme was an error of law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the County Court on a point of law under section 204 Housing Act 1996 following review of suitability of accommodation offered under section 193.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed with costs; November 2003 review decision quashed and fresh review ordered.
enrichment.ratio: A homelessness suitability reviewer must consider facts known at the date of review, including changes since the original offer; where a council must allocate under its published scheme, failure to consider eligibility under that scheme when deciding suitability is an error of law even if accommodation might otherwise be broadly suitable.
legal_issues: Whether review facts are those at offer date or review date
Whether omission of the child's age and allocation policy was an error of law
Whether eligibility under the allocation scheme is relevant to suitability

enrichment.short_title: London Borough of Sutton v S: school attendance reasonable justification
key_facts: Parents were prosecuted under section 444(1A) after their 14-year-old daughter K attended school only 29 of 174 days.
Magistrates found parents knew of non-attendance, co-operated with welfare officers and parenting support, but could not overcome K's breakdown and overwhelming needs.
Magistrates acquitted under section 444(1A) for reasonable justification and declined to convict under section 444(1) via section 444(8B).
Sutton appealed by case stated seeking guidance on reasonable justification and section 444(8B) discretion.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Administrative Court appeal by case stated from magistrates' acquittal on school attendance charges.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; court declined to give broad guidance where issues were factual, respondents unrepresented, and appeal hopeless on findings.
enrichment.ratio: On the magistrates' findings the parents' reasonable justification defence under section 444(1A) raised no issue of law; Fairbanks principles apply by analogy to section 444(8B) alternative verdict discretion but remittal was inappropriate here.
legal_issues: Whether the magistrates' findings could amount to reasonable justification
Scope of reasonable justification under section 444(1A)
Exercise of discretion under section 444(8B) after acquittal on the greater offence

enrichment.short_title: Turkey v Awadh: stay and security for costs after undue influence trial
key_facts: Following a 14-day trial Cooke J ordered transfer of 141 Inverness Terrace to Mr Turkey and £34,000 costs on account from his daughter Aziza.
Aziza appealed with permission and sought a stay of execution; parties agreed arrangements preserving the property pending appeal.
Staughton LJ granted a stay of the £34,000 payment but refused an order requiring payment into court.
Security for appeal costs of £15,000 was ordered payable by 4 January 2005 given Saudi residence and substantial assets.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application in the Court of Appeal for stay of execution and security for costs pending appeal from undue influence judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Payment-into-court application refused; stay granted on the £34,000 order; £15,000 security for appeal costs ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Stay and security turn on risk of injustice; where the appellant would not pay in any event, payment-into-court conditions may unfairly stifle appeal, but security for costs may still be ordered where the appellant is abroad and has means, even if individual impecuniosity alone is insufficient post-Nasser.
legal_issues: Whether execution of the costs payment should be stayed or paid into court
Whether security for costs should be ordered against an individual resident in Saudi Arabia
Appropriate quantum of security for appeal costs

enrichment.short_title: Dacre Son & Hartley v North Yorkshire Trading Standards: property misdescription informations
key_facts: Estate agent Dacre Son & Hartley was convicted of two section 1 offences over statements to undercover purchasers about damp at 9 Riverside Walk, Airton.
Mrs Hickman had previously withdrawn after discovering serious damp and supplied an independent report; employee Miss Cuerden denied or downplayed damp on 28 August and 4 September 2002.
The firm challenged informations for insufficient particularisation and argued no case to answer at the close of the prosecution case.
Justices convicted on two counts; the Administrative Court upheld informations and evidence sufficiency.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from Skipton magistrates' convictions under the Property Misdescriptions Act 1991.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; justices' approach upheld; respondent awarded £4,800 costs on summary assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Informations under Rule 100 Magistrates' Courts Rules 1981 need not name the employee where the business is charged under section 1(1); advance information and trial evidence may cure lack of particularisation if no real unfairness; challenges to particulars should usually be raised before trial rather than via no-case submissions.
legal_issues: Adequacy of informations under Rule 100
Use of advance information and trial evidence to supply particulars
Sufficiency of evidence for strict liability misdescription offences

enrichment.short_title: North Star Shipping v Sphere Drake: strike-out of sue and labour claim
key_facts: War risks insurers disputed a constructive total loss claim after a bomb damaged the NORTH STAR at Piraeus in July 1994.
Owners also claimed sue and labour expenses of about US$459,168 detailed in a June 1995 letter but never properly pleaded.
Writ and points of claim referred to sue and labour in general terms without identifying measures, reasonableness or costs.
At trial commencement insurers declined to cross-examine on sue and labour; Colman J struck out that head of claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory ruling during Commercial Court trial on whether sue and labour expenses could be pursued.
enrichment.outcome: Sue and labour element of re-amended points of claim struck out as too late and unfair to insurers.
enrichment.ratio: A sue and labour claim under Institute Time Clauses is a distinct cause of action requiring pleading of the averting measures, their reasonableness and cost; after years of proceedings without particulars or a final schedule, allowing amendment mid-trial would cause serious prejudice.
legal_issues: Whether sue and labour was adequately pleaded
Whether amendment or particulars could be permitted during trial
Prejudice to insurers from late sue and labour case

enrichment.short_title: Cummings v Cardiff: taxi licence lottery and delimitation judicial review
key_facts: Cardiff controlled hackney carriage numbers and resolved in January 2003 to issue six licences by lottery among existing licence holders.
Mr Cummings, controlling 58 vehicles, challenged the lottery; the council later rescinded it and delimited licence numbers in October 2003.
The January committee report misdescribed the waiting list history, leading to rejection of date-order allocation.
Moses J found the January report misleading on the waiting list but upheld October delimitation as lawful and unrelated to allocation method defects.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Two linked judicial review claims challenging Cardiff's lottery decision and subsequent delimitation decision.
enrichment.outcome: Both applications refused; council awarded costs of JR2; claimant awarded costs of JR1 up to 7 October 2003; permission to appeal and stay refused.
enrichment.ratio: A misleading committee report on waiting list use can flaw a lottery decision, but defects in a rescinded January decision do not taint a later delimitation decision if delimitation was considered on its own merits without treating allocation methods as a relevant comparator.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of allocating hackney licences by lottery
Whether the committee report misled members about the waiting list
Whether January process defects tainted October delimitation

enrichment.short_title: R v Grant: severance and Watson direction in door-staff murder trial
key_facts: Mr Grant, a Yates Wine Lodge customer, was convicted of murdering accountant Naresh Shah during a retaliatory attack on the wrong address after a prior pub incident.
Co-defendant door staff were acquitted of murder but convicted of conspiracy to cause GBH; Grant also convicted on that count.
After Grant identified Rafiq as knife-wielder, co-accused cross-examined him on a prior Indian restaurant incident involving two knives; severance was refused.
The judge directed the jury to disregard Indian restaurant evidence against Grant and later gave a modified Watson direction after prolonged deliberations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) appeal against murder and conspiracy convictions with leave on severance and Watson direction grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; severance refusal and Watson direction upheld as fair.
enrichment.ratio: In cut-throat trials similar-fact evidence admissible between co-accused cannot be excluded by discretion; severance is exceptional and was not warranted where the judge directed the jury to ignore prejudicial evidence against Grant; minor additions to a Watson direction do not render convictions unsafe where verdicts were unanimous after further deliberation.
legal_issues: Whether the trial judge should have severed Grant's trial after Indian restaurant evidence
Fairness under Article 6 where co-accused cross-examine on propensity evidence
Whether modified Watson direction created undue pressure on the jury

enrichment.short_title: Topplan v Townley: adverse possession and 1993 road works interruption
key_facts: David Townley farmed 13 acres near Scotforth under grazing licences until 1982 then continued use without payment, treating the land as part of Whinney Carr Farm.
Topplan became registered proprietor in 1992; in 1993 Lancashire County Council widened the A6, taking a road strip and temporarily using a working area under licence.
Townley did not protest the road works to avoid alerting the owner while limitation time ran.
Lloyd J held adverse possession succeeded except for the temporary working area; the Court of Appeal dismissed Topplan's appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against County Palatine judgment on adverse possession and rectification of registered title.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; squatter entitled to registration except working area strip.
enrichment.ratio: Following Pye, adverse possession requires factual possession and intention to possess, not hostility to the paper owner; prior grazing licences do not negate later possession after holdover; limited owner-authorized entry on part of the land for road works does not interrupt possession of the remainder, and a squatter need not alert the owner that time is running.
legal_issues: Whether post-licence farming amounted to factual possession from 1983
Whether April 1993 road works interrupted adverse possession under Schedule 1 paragraph 8(2)
Whether silent acquiescence negated animus possidendi
